summary: Proposes using 31-bit subnet masks on IPv4 point-to-point links, so a link uses two addresses instead of four. This halves the address space used for such links, a small change that saves addresses. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A road between exactly two houses only needs two house numbers, not four. This lets network links use just two addresses and saves the rest.

questions: can i use a /31 on a point to point link
how many addresses does a point to point link need
why is directed broadcast not possible on a /31
subtitle: How a point-to-point IPv4 link can use a /31 subnet and spend two addresses instead of four.

tldr.problem: Numbered point-to-point links in IPv4 normally use a 30-bit subnet mask, which burns four addresses on a link that only has two endpoints and no use for broadcast.
tldr.mechanism: A 31-bit mask leaves a one-bit host number, and the two resulting addresses must be treated as host addresses, with the limited broadcast used for any broadcast traffic on the link.
tldr.outcome: Each link consumes two addresses instead of four, and the RFC rewrites the affected rules in the host and router requirements documents. The router vendors and ISPs it mentions reported no problems in testing.

today: RFC 3021 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself describes its recommendations as already implemented in beta code by several router vendors at the time of writing.

sections.title: Why Save Addresses on Links
sections.content:
The RFC starts from the pressure to conserve IP address space. It lists the existing responses: stricter allocation guidelines, Network Address Translators, and a new Internet Protocol (IPv6, which it says has not yet seen production deployment). While waiting for a larger address space, it looks for small changes to current practice.

One such change is how point-to-point links are numbered. Leaving the links unnumbered is used in some parts of the Internet, but it makes the link hard to manage and debug, means a router cannot be reached through it consistently, and lacks standardization. Using host addresses on both ends works only with PPP encapsulation and can put the two ends in different networks, which complicates management.

With the usual 30-bit mask, a link uses four addresses: two hosts, one all-zeros network address and one all-ones broadcast address. A point-to-point link has only two endpoints and no real notion of broadcast, because anything sent by one end is received by the other.
sections.plainLanguage: Giving every little two-house road four house numbers wastes numbers. The RFC asks whether two would do, since only two houses are on the road.

sections.title: Two Addresses From a 31-Bit Mask
sections.content:
The RFC reads an address as <Network-number><Host-number>, where the host number is the unmasked part and SHOULD be at least 1 bit wide. A 31-bit subnet mask leaves a host number of only one bit, so only two addresses are possible: the network number followed by 0, and the network number followed by all ones (written -1).

Historically those two values meant the network address and the directed broadcast. On a point-to-point link with a 31-bit mask, the RFC says they MUST be interpreted as host addresses, one for each end of the link.

The saving is easy to count. Each link takes two addresses instead of four, so a network with 500 point-to-point links saves 1000 addresses, which the RFC equates to four class C address spaces. The RFC assumes a routing system that can do classless (CIDR) routing, and it notes that earlier subnetting documentation had already hinted at a one-bit host-number field.
sections.plainLanguage: With only one digit left for the house number, there are just two numbers, 0 and 1. Normally those would be special, but here each house on the road simply uses one.

sections.title: Broadcast Handling and Routing Impact
sections.content:
The RFC lists the historically recognized broadcast forms. The directed broadcast is the network number followed by all ones, and the network number followed by zero is an obsolete form of it that older hosts may still use. The limited (link-local) broadcast is all ones, with all zeros as an obsolete form.

Because a 31-bit prefix leaves only the two host addresses, a directed broadcast to the link is no longer possible. The limited broadcast MUST be used for all broadcast traffic on such a link. The decision on whether a destination is a directed broadcast is made by the router directly connected to the destination segment, so forwarding in remote routers is not affected.

Routing protocols are not affected either. Most deployed protocols already support classless routing, and exchanges between peers use multicast, limited broadcast or unicast addresses on the local network, none of which change. The RFC covers only point-to-point links and does not consider other interface types.

Losing the directed broadcast on these links is seen by the RFC as a side benefit, since it slightly improves resistance to a class of denial of service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: On a two-house road, shouting to everybody is the same as talking to the other house. So the only shout allowed is the general one to the whole neighbourhood, and the special street-wide shout goes away.

sections.title: Edits to Existing Standards
sections.content:
Section 3 lists the changes the idea makes to three published documents. In each, the rule against using the directed broadcast or subnetwork address as a source is relaxed for one case: the originator is an endpoint of a point-to-point link with a 31-bit mask.

  • RFC 1122 (host requirements): item (e) is replaced, and a new item (h) for the subnetwork number is added. It SHOULD NOT be used as a source address except on such a link; elsewhere a packet with such a destination SHOULD be silently discarded, and if not discarded it MUST be treated as an IP broadcast.
  • Assigned Numbers (RFC 1700): the directed broadcast form may also be a source address when the originator is an endpoint of such a link.
  • RFC 1812 (router requirements): item (d) is replaced, folding in the update from RFC 2644, and a new item (f) is added. Several rules in section 4.2.3.1 are replaced, and a note is added to section 4.3.3.9.

On a 31-bit link, a packet addressed to the network prefix followed by -1, or followed by 0, corresponds to one of the link's endpoints and MUST be treated as directed to the router that has that address. The router's configuration of such a mask SHOULD allow it to generate datagrams addressed to the prefix followed by 0. Broadcast Address Mask Replies on these links MUST use 255.255.255.255.
sections.plainLanguage: The rulebook said never to use certain special numbers as your own. The RFC adds a small exception for the two ends of a short link.

sections.title: Operational Experience and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC reports that several router vendors had implemented the recommendations in beta code, and that at least three ISPs tested it with positive results and no problems found. The routing protocols tested successfully were OSPF, IS-IS, BGP and EIGRP. It expected an official release within a few months and adoption by other vendors.

The RFC includes one deployment warning: a point-to-point link where only one end supports 31-bit prefixes may not operate correctly. So both ends of a link need to agree on the scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: Both ends of the road must agree to use the new two-number way. If only one end does, they may not understand each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security discussion is about denial of service attacks that rely on packet replication through directed broadcasts, the kind known as smurf attacks. Using 31-bit subnet masks in the core of the Internet reduces the number of physical links on which such an attack can be launched, because a 31-bit link has no directed broadcast.

The RFC concludes that implementing its recommendation improves the Internet's resilience to these attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: If nobody can shout to a whole street from far away, nobody can use that trick to flood the street with noise.
